# Introduction and Setup

## Why are we here?

By the end of this hour you will be able to:

- Explain what [version control]{.uwred} is and why it matters for data science
- Put a project folder under Git and track changes to it
- Save versions with meaningful messages, and look back at your history
- Tell Git to ignore files it should not track
- Push your work to [GitHub]{.uwred} to back it up and share it

<div class="gap-md"></div>

We will build one project together, start to finish: [Bucky's game-day menu]{.uwred}.

<div class="gap-md"></div>

You'll build this repo along with me the whole hour — including the [Your turn]{.uwred} moments, where you try a step on your own before we regroup.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## What is version control?

[Version control]{.uwred} keeps track of changes you make to files over time.

<div class="gap-sm"></div>

It lets you:

- Go back to any earlier version of a file
- Keep only [one]{.uwred} copy in your folder (not ten copies with different names)
- See what changed, when, and why
- Work with others without emailing files back and forth
- Keep the same project synced across computers


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## You have probably done this the hard way

How many of these folders have you lived in?

<div class="gap-sm"></div>

```
analysis.R
analysis_v2.R
analysis_final.R
analysis_final_FINAL.R
analysis_2026-10-01.R
analysis_2026-10-01_jjc.R
```

<div class="gap-sm"></div>

You cannot tell what changed between any two of them, and they all pile up in the same folder.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Git fixes this

With Git, you keep [one]{.uwred} `analysis.R` in your folder.

<div class="gap-sm"></div>

Git quietly stores the full history behind the scenes. At any point you can:

- Ask "what did this file look like last Tuesday?"
- Read the note you left yourself explaining each change
- Restore an older version without losing your current work

<div class="gap-md"></div>

> "Your closest collaborator is you six months ago, and they don't answer email."

Git is how you leave notes for that person.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Git is not GitHub

A point of confusion worth clearing up right away:

<div class="gap-sm"></div>

<table>
<thead>
<tr>
  <th></th>
  <th>What it is</th>
  <th>Where it lives</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
  <td><strong>Git</strong></td>
  <td>The version-control software</td>
  <td>On your computer</td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td><strong>GitHub</strong></td>
  <td>A website that hosts Git repositories</td>
  <td>In the cloud</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

<div class="gap-md"></div>

You can use Git with no internet at all. [GitHub]{.uwred} is where you put a copy to back it up, share it, and collaborate. We get there at the end of the hour.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Our running example: Bucky's game-day menu

[Bucky Badger]{.uwred} is planning the food for a game-day tailgate, and the menu keeps changing.

<div class="gap-sm"></div>

We will keep the plan in a folder called `gameday-menu`, with a file per part of the spread:

- `brats.txt`
- `cheese_curds.txt`
- `desserts.txt`

<div class="gap-sm"></div>

As the menu evolves, we will use Git to track every change, so Bucky can always see what the plan looked like last week.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## What you should already have

This lecture assumes three things are done:

1. [Git is installed]{.uwred} on your laptop
2. You have a [GitHub account]{.uwred}
3. You have an SSH key set up to validate your identity with Github

<div class="gap-sm"></div>

If these are not yet done, see Appendices A & B now, and then catch up with a neighbor:

<div class="gap-md"></div>

Everything today happens in a [terminal]{.uwred} (Git Bash on Windows; Terminal on macOS/Linux). Git commands all start with the word `git`.

<div class="gap-md"></div>

RStudio also has a built in terminal.  I use it rather than a separate terminal for git and file management when I am working on analysis code for a project.  Its up to you!


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Tell Git who you are

Git stamps every saved version with a name and email. Set yours [once per computer]{.uwred}:

<div class="gap-sm"></div>

```bash
git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "you@wisc.edu"
```

<div class="gap-sm"></div>

Use [your own]{.uwred} name and email, not Bucky's. The email should match the one on your GitHub account.

The `--global` flag means "use this for every project on this computer," so you only do it once.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Check that it worked

You can confirm your settings at any time:

<div class="gap-sm"></div>

```bash
git config --list
```

<div class="gap-sm"></div>

Look for your `user.name` and `user.email` in the output:

```
user.name=Bucky Badger
user.email=bucky@wisc.edu
init.defaultBranch=main
```

<div class="gap-sm"></div>

If you made a typo, just run the `config` command again to overwrite it.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Make a folder for the project

Create a folder for Bucky's menu and move into it.  

<div class="gap-md"></div>

I prefer to keep all of my git repos at one location (`~/github`)

<div class="gap-sm"></div>

```bash
cd
mkdir github
cd github

mkdir gameday-menu
cd gameday-menu
```

<div class="gap-sm"></div>

Right now this is just an ordinary folder. Git is not watching it yet.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Turn the folder into a repository

A [repository]{.uwred} (or "repo") is a folder that Git is tracking, along with its full history.

<div class="gap-sm"></div>

Turn the current folder into one with a single command:

```bash
git init
```

<div class="gap-sm"></div>

```
Initialized empty Git repository in /home/github/gameday-menu/.git/
```

<div class="gap-sm"></div>

Git created a hidden `.git` folder to store the history. You never edit it by hand; Git manages it for you.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Meet `git status`

`git status` is the command you will run the most. It tells you where things stand.

<div class="gap-sm"></div>

```bash
git status
```

<div class="gap-sm"></div>

```
On branch main
No commits yet
nothing to commit (create/copy files and use "git add" to track)
```


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Reading that message

Three things Git just told us:

<div class="gap-sm"></div>

- [On branch main]{.uwred} — the default line of work (more on branches another day)
- [No commits yet]{.uwred} — we have no saved history in this repo
- [nothing to commit]{.uwred} — the folder is empty, so there is nothing to track

<div class="gap-md"></div>

Notice the hint: *use "git add" to track*. Git is telling us the next step.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Where we are

We have:

- Confirmed Git knows who we are
- Created the `gameday-menu` folder
- Turned it into a Git repository with `git init`
- Learned to check in with `git status`

<div class="gap-md"></div>
